Review of LNG projects 
*102. SHR! ASHWANI KUMAR: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
 
 
 
 
 
1 
 

RAJYA  SABHA [26 November, 2002] 
(a) what would be the impact of the gas discovered by the Reliance/ NIKO 
consortium on the viability of the LNG projects currently under finalisation 
and whether Government propose to review the LNG projects in vrew of the 
new found gas resources; and 
(b) how much tin-.e would be required for commercializing the natural gas 
discoveries in Vizag and Surat? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUIVI AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (b) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) As per the Hydrocarbon Vision 2025 the demand of Natural Gas is 
estimated to be 231 million standard cubic meters per day (MMSCMD) in 2006-
07. The current supply is only around 65 MMSCMD.The major gas discovery 
by the consortium of Reliance Industries Ltd., and Nlko Resources Ltd., 
Canada in the KG—DWN-98/3 block in Krishna-Godavari off-shore basin on the 
East Coast Is expected to produce 25-35 MMSCMD of gas as per the estimates of 
the consortium. The expected production by Niko Resources Ltd., from the 
discovery near Surat on land block-CB-ONN-2000/2 in Gujarat has not been 
firmed up. Despite the additionality in gas supply there will remain a large gap 
between demand and supply. This may be met by import of (a) gas through 
pipeline and (b) Liquefied Natural Gas (L.N.G.). However, LNG Is under Open 
General Licence (OGL) list and the import initiatives will be propelled by 
commercial viability of the respective project. 
(b) Development plans and schedule of commercial production in 
respect of these discoveries have not been firmed up by the concerned 
companies. 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir. my question was very specific—What is 
going to be the impact of the gas discovery on the current LNG Projects on the 
way? Now, the answer, that has been given by the hon. Minister, says that there 
is still a large gap between the demand and the supply, and that this is required 
to be bridged either by import of gas through pipeline or through LNG prelects. 
Now, as per the answer, since the LNG is under the OGL, the viability of the 
project wuuld depend upon the commercial feasibility. My specific question 
was: Are the current LNG projects, in view of the gas discovery, going to be 
continuously viable or

[26 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
not? So, Sir, the specific answer has no t come to my specific question. Then, 
as far as answer to the second question, regarding the commercial production 
of the gas discoveries, is concerned, the answer has been given that the 
companies have not firmed It up. I would like to know from the hon. Minister 
whether the Director-General of Hydrocar bons Is under a duty to ensure that 
they are implementable. The question is , what is, at least, the anticipatory 
time frame for specific programme for the development and 
commercialisation of the gas? 
SHRI RAM NAIK: Sir, I have given the required information, but I 
would certainly like to supplement the information. Even before 
supplementing the information, I would like to take an opportunity to inform 
the House that under the new exploration licensing policy, through which 
these two discoveries have taken place,  the first discovery of Reliance has 
been under the first round of the block, awarded under the new Exploration 
Licensing Policy. The second, at Surat,  under the NICO, has been under the 
second round of the exploration block. So, I would say that the new policy 
that has been taken up has started yielding good results. Only yesterday, the 
third round has been finalised. We have finalised 23 blocks. And, with this, in 
the last three years, we have given 70 blocks for exploration. We have now 
given 23 blocks also. With that, in regard to the specific point on which the 
hon. Member has put a question, I have already said that the Hydrocarbon 
Vision—2025, a policy document of the Government, indicates that by the 
year 2006—I am taking up the period of Five Year Plan also—231 million 
MMSCMD will be the estimated demand. Against that, the present supply 
position is just 65 million MMSCMD. So, there is a gap of nearly 166 million 
MMSCMD. With this discovery also, a wide gap is still continuing. That is 
why the remaining gap can be filled by more discoveries which will come in 
future in our country, and also through the pipelines from the other countries 
that we are presently working out. However, no final decision has been taken 
in this regard. A decision has been taken in regard to the import of LNG. We 
have entered into a contract with Qatar, and will be getting that LNG gas by 
the end of next year. As I have been saying that the gas is thp energy of the 21 
St Century, more and more gas is required. And, this gap is being bridged by 
present two discoveries.The discovery of gas by the Reliance had been 
declared onjiy on 29th October, 2002. After they inform the Director-General 
of Hydrocarbons, the Committee starts the plan that has

at Surat is concerned, which is on land block, it had been discovered only in 
the first week of November. It will take some time. So far, fhey have drilled 
only one well. They will drill some more wells. Only then, they would be in a 
position to say how much gas would be available. Once that is anticipated, only 
then other things can follow.

Economic growth 
668. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND  
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the average economic growth in the past three 
years has been only 4 per cent compared to 7.5 per cent in the years 1994—
97; 
(b) whether Government have identified the causes for this poor 
performance; and 
(c) if so, the strategies drawn up to improve performance? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) As per 
the Central Statistical Organisation, the average growrth in Gross Domestic Product 
(GDP) at constant {1993-94 prices) during 1994-95 to 1996-97 was 7.5 per 
cent compared with 5.1 per cent during 1999-2000 to 2001 -02. 
(b) The lower growth in GDP during 1999-2000 to 2001-02 has been 
mainly due to lower average growth in agriculture and allied sector, mining and 
quarrying as also in some of the service sectors. 
(c) The Government is conscious of the need for higher economic 
growth. The Union Budget for 2002-03 adopted a six-pronged strategy, inter-
atia. emphasising continuation of agricultural and food economy reforms, 
enhancement of public and private investment in infrastructure, strengthening the 
financial sector and capital markets, deepening structural reforms and regenerating 
industrial grov/th. The various reform measures are expected to have a positive 
effect on the growth of the economy.

COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) In 
September 2001, RBI announced the guidelines in terms of which banks were 
permitted on an experimental basis, to extend finance to stockbrokers for margin 
trading within the overall ceiling of 5% prescribed for exposure of banks to 
capital market, for a period of 60 days. These guidelines were reviewed by the

exchange and would be allotted a uni que client code for use across the 
market. The proposals provide for a separate margin trading guarantee 
fund. The stock exchange shall undertake risk management measures

119

Mention Account";

to the tune of Rs. one lakh crores? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has circulated guidelines to all 
commercial banks for prevention of slippage of non-performing assets (NPAs) 
accounts from "sub-standard" category to "doubtful/loss" category, which include 
suggestions on "Early Alert System" and "Special Mention Accounts". The 
"Early Alert System" envisages that the banks put in place a system that 
captures early warning signals in respect of accounts showing first signs of 
weakness so that timely and adequate interventions can be made to reverse the 
position. Under this system a new asset category once the earliest signs of 
sickness/irregularities are noticed. Accounts classified under this category 
would not be treated as NPAs and would not require provisioning. 
(c) Government of India and RBI have advised the Banks and 
Financial Institutions to take several steps for recovery of dues such as evolving 
and the implementation of recovery policy by banks, compromise settlement 
through Settlement Advisory Committees and filing of suits in Debt Recovery 
Tribunals (DRTs). Banks have also been advised to use the forum of Lok 
Adalat for compromise settlements. RBI in July, 2002 and also introduced non-
discretionary andtion-discriminatory One Time Settlement Scheme for NPAs 
upto Rs. 5 crore. 
Credit Information Bureau has been set up to disseminate information on 
borrowers to the Banks. Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR) scheme has been 
put in place to provide a transparent mechanism for restructuring of corporate debts 
to viable entitles facing problems due to internal and external factors. Further, 
to facilitate foreclosures and enforcement of securities in cases of default and 
to enable the banks and financial institutions to realize their dues, "The 
Securitlsation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of

Inter-State Water Crisis 
749. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact, that India has enough water to take care of every 
State need; 
(b) if so. the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that inter-State crisis over the use of this water 
resource is increasing every-year; and 
(d) if so, the details of the steps, Government propose to take to solve 
the inter-State river water disputes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) As per the 
latest assessment {1993) made by Central Water Commission (CWC), the average 
annual water availability in the river-system of the country is assessed at 1869 
Billion Cubic Meter (BCM). The availability of water is assessed river basin-
wise. The per capita water availability in  the year 2001 is 1820 cubic metre 
per year on a national level. The lowest per capita average availability of 
water in the country is estimated as 298 cubic metre annually in Sabarmati basin 
and the highest per capita average availability of water in the country is 
estimated as 16,990 cubic metre 
163 

RAJYA  SABHA [26 November, 2002] 
annually in Minto River Basins Draining into Bangladesh & Mayanmar 
followed by 13,636 cubic metre annually In Brahmaputra-Barak Sub-basin. 
(c) The Ravi and Beas Water Dispute between the State of Punjab, 
Haryana and Rajasthan and Cauvery Water Disputes between the States of 
Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and P ondicherry were referred to Tribunals 
under the provisions of Inter State Water Dispute (ISWD) Act, 1956 in April, 
1986 and June 1990 respectively. The Central Government in 2002 has 
received requests under Section 3 of the said Act from the States of Goa and 
Karnataka respectively for referring to the Tribunals the disputes relating to 
sharing of water of Mahadayi/ Madevi river and sharing of surplus water of 
Krishna river for adjudication and decision. 
(d) The Central Government endeavours to resolve the dispute by 
negotiations, failing which the dispute is referred to a Tribunal at the request of party 
States as per the provision of ISWD Act, 1956 for adjudication. The said Act 
has been amended on March 28, 2002 to provide for time-bound adjudication of 
disputes by the Tribunals. Also as pe r the amended Act, the decision of the 
Tribunal, after its publication in the Official Gazette, shall have the same force as 
an order or decree of the Supreme Court.

purposes?

RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b)

conservation and preservation of water resources, optimal utilization of the 
existing water resources infrastructure , development of new resources with 
active participation of all the stakeholders in 
164 

[26 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
various facets of water resources ma nagement. The policy further provides 
for inter basin transfer of river w/ater from the flood prone areas to the water 
scarce areas. These measures aim at sustainable and equitable development of 
water resources and water security in the country. 
There is an average annual precipita tion {Including snowfall) of 4000 
Billion Cubic Metre (BCM) in the country. Out of this, the annual average 
flow in the river systems of the count ry Is 1869 BCM. Th e utillzable surface

DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether share of States spending on water management is declining 
sharply, as reported in the Economic Times dated the 5th August, 2002; 
(b) if so, whether there has been considerable less rainfall during the current 
year; 
(c) if so, whether this has further aggravated the shortage of water in 
many States; 
(d) whether the National Water Policy adopted by Government has failed 
to provide right climate for private sector participation in this sector; and 
(e) if so, the steps Government propose to take to implement the other 
recommendations of the National Water Policy to meet the water shortage? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY); (a) There has been a 
consistent increase in the plan-wise outlays (in absolute terms) for water 
management that encompasses Irrigation, command area development and flood 
control activities. However, percentage share of public investment including States' 
share in water management in relation to the total investment has consistently 
declined from 23% in the first plan to about 6% in the Ninth Plan as indicated

spell of 14 good monsoons that followed the previous all-India drought year of 
1987. The monsoon rainfall (June-September) for the 
167

country as a whole was 19% below normal. 29% area of the country 
experienced drought conditions with 19%  area under moderate category and 
10% under severe category. 
(c) The average per capita water availability at present in the country is 1820 
cubic metre per year as against the international criteria of annual water 
availability of less than 1000 cubic metre per capita which is considered as 
scarcity condition. However, due to the spatial variability of rain in the country 
and also because of variation in population density, per capita average annual 
availability of water in different basins presently varies from 13, 636 cubic 
metre in Brahmaputra-Barak basin to 298 cubic metre in Sabarmati basin. The 
temporal variability in the rainfall also creates temporary scarcity of water in 
certain years. The less rainfall during the current year has resulted in water 
shortage in certain parts of the country where rainfall was for below normal. 
(d) The National Water Policy, 2002 provides that private sector 
participation should be encouraged in planning, development and 
management of water resources projects for diverse uses wherever feasible. 
(e) The National Water Policy, 2002 provides that each State shall 
formulate its own State Water Policy back ed with an operational Action Plan 
in a time bound manner, say in two years to achieve the desired objectives of 
the Policy including meeting the water shortage. After adoption of the 
National Water Policy in April, 2002, several steps have been taken for Its 
implementation.These include inter-ministerial meetings with Central and State 
Governments, interaction with Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) and 
institutions concerned with the water sector. A series of seven regional Workshops 
was also organised by the Ministry of Water Resources at various places in the 
country during August to October, 2002 for continued deliberations with the 
NGOs, water experts and professionals. The Action Plan will be placed in the 
Conference of Water Resources and Irrigation Ministers of States and Union 
Territory Administrations for its consider ation and thereafter sent to all State 
Governments and concerned Central Ministries for implementation.

755. SHRI R. P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES 
be pleased state: 
(a) whether a fresh review has been undertaken to assess the availability 
of utilisable water and its demand in the country in the wake of recent drought in 
several parts of the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that with the present rate of growth in population the 
demand for utilisable water for domestic industrial and agricultural purposes 
would out-strip its supply, reaching critical famine conditions by 2025 A.D.; and 
(d) if so, the details of the long term plans drawn up to ensure better 
management of water resources and other research based practical and 
affordable solutions? 
170 

[26 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) No, Sir. As 
per the latest assessment made the utilisable surface water is assessed as 690 Billion 
Cubic Metre (BCM), the annual replenishable ground water resource is about 
432 BCM, totaling to 1122 BCM. This utilizable flow is out of total availability 
of water of 1869 BCM. On an average the total water resources availability in 
the country remains the same although the spatial and temporal variability of 
rain in the country creates temporary scarcity of water in certain years. The 
drought conditions in certain parts of the country during the current year is a 
result of less rainfall this year. 
(c) Owing to increase in population, urbanization and better living 
standards the demand of water for diverse uses has been estimated for the year 
2025 AD as 1093 BCM out of which 73 BCM is for domestic. 23 BCM is for 
industrial, 910 BCM is for irrigation (Agriculture), 15 BCM is for energy and 72 
BCM is for other uses. The projected demand of water for the year 2025 will be 
possible to meet by exploiting almost all the 1122 BCM of utilizable water by 
conventional means. 
(d) Through concerted efforts of State Governments, an irrigation 
potential of approximately 95.40 million hectares has been created by the end of 
9th Five Year Plan. This has been possible due to construction of 3596 major 
and medium projects providing 177 BCM of storage of rain water. Another 
207.7 BCM of storage is likely to be created through ongoing and proposed projects. 
To help the State Governments in their efforts to harness the water from natural 
resources and accelerate creation of irrigation potential by early completion of 
ongoing schemes, Government of Indi a has launched Accelerated Irrigation 
Benefits Programme (AIBP) since 1996-97. Under the programme, financial 
assistance In the form of central loan is being extended to State Governments to 
help them complete the ongoing irrigation projects in a time bound manner so that 
the benefits could accrue at the earliest. Accordingly, the Central Loan Assistant 
(CLA) amounting to Rs. 8480 crore to the State Governments have been provided 
under AIBP upto end of 2001-02. An outlay of Rs. 2800 crore has been 
provided for the year 2002-03. An amount of Rs. 594.75 crore has been released 
duhng current year upto 31.10.2002.

Watershed Management Programme, artificial recharge of ground water and 
roof-top rain water han/esting under the sectoral reform project of

MNC's right over water 
†763. SHRI JANESHWAR IV1ISHRA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Multi National Companies are acquiring the 
rights over water instead of that of the community; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the Central Government and other State 
Governments are also contemplating to privatize this sector; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (d) No, Sir. 
The rights over water are not being given to Multi National Companies. The 
National Water Policy envisages inolvement of stakeholders, Non-
Governmental Organisations and the private sector in planning, development 
and management of water sources. As laid down in the policy, the water 
supply and sewerage services in some of the mega cities are being 
contemplated by some of the State Governments to be given to the Corporate 
Sector on lease basis for management and improvement of service efficiency.

Depletion of Groundwater in Andhra Pradesh 
DR. T SUBBARAMI REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the mapping done 
by the National Remote Sensing Agency to find out the ground water prospects 
for Andhra Pradesh, indicates that ground water reservoirs are fast depleting. 
Sir, NRSA took 300 aerial maps of the State and discovered that Andhra 
Pradesh is a 'problematic' State owing to its rocky terrain. This is the first time that 
a combination of satellite inputs and ground inputs have been used for mapping 
which is more accurate than the ground inputs used in the past. The only 
solution to improve the ground water level is to take up a massive programme for 
recharging the ground water Sir, NRSA has prepared 1723 maps for six States, 
including 300 maps for Andhra Pradesh. The Agency has mapped Andhra 
Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and 
Jharkhand. The study revealed that all the seven States are problematic as 
regards the ground water situation because of rocky terrain. These maps have 
been prepared under a three-year programme, s ponsored by the Ministry of 
Rural Development, in technical collaboration with the ISRO. Therefore, the 
Ministry should take up a massive programme tor recharging the ground water in 
the State of Andhra Pradesh and in other six States urgently to solve the ground 
water problem.

Prevention of Thaiassaemia in the country 
SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE (West Bengal): Sir. Thaiassaemia is a 
dreaded genetic disease. According to the World Health Organisation (1997) 
statistics, about 26,000 children in India are born every year, with this disease. It is 
estimated that one-fourth of the total Thalassamic babies in the world are born in 
our country. The cost of treatment of each patient is roughly estimated at Rs. 1.5 
Rs.-1.75 lakhs per annum. 
To eradicate this disease, pre-marriage counselling is the only 
alternative. If a carrier of this disease does not marry another carrier of this 
disease, then prevention can become very simple. Thaiassaemia can be 
fought only with awareness and resulting consciousness. Due to lackofawarness 
in our country, the number of affected births is regularly increasing. Many of the 
Mediterranean coutries have eradicated the disease through awareness 
programmes and by enacting suitable legislation, compulsory blood examination 
of both males and females before marriage.

The Govenment of India should also initiate massive popular awareness 
campaigns to eradicate this disease.
